newsitem.title: USA: US CORPORATE BONDS - Chrysler, McLead price debt.
newsitem.headline: US CORPORATE BONDS - Chrysler, McLead price debt.

text.p: New issues such as Chrysler Corp's $500 million offering of century bonds and McLeodUSA Inc's $225 million junk bond offering, grabbed the spotlight in the U.S. corporate bond market on Tuesday, market players said.
Secondary market trading of both high-yield and investment-grade bonds was muted on Tuesday, as investors looked to the primary market for value.
"Retail (trading) activity has been real quiet," said a high-grade bond trader. "Buyers have been hesitant because spreads have tightened again."
Chrysler sold $500 million in 100-year debentures, non-callable in 90 years, via Salomon Brothers Inc.
The debt (A3/A) priced to yield 7.406 percent, a level which a trader away from the deal called "fair."
Chrysler became one of a number of issuers, such as Federal Express Corp, to price 100-year deals in recent weeks in order to capitalize on strong investor demand for long-duration securities.
In the junk bond market, McLeodUSA, a competitive local exchange carrier based in the midwest U.S., was the first of several telecom offerings expected to price this week.

McLeod increased the size of its offering to $225 million from an original size of $175 million in response to strong investor interest. The bonds, priced at par to yield 9.25 percent, were heard trading at 101 later in the day.

Telecommunications offerings expected later this week include MetroNet Communications' $200 million 144a offering, American Communications Services' $170 million 144a deal, and GCI Holdings $150 million public deal.
Other junk issues to price on Tuesday were Discovery Zone Inc's $80 million unit offering and Mexican wireless telephone company Grupo Iusacell SA de CV's IUSI.MX $150 million deal.

In other news, senior notes of Merisel Inc dropped around 10 points from an opening level of 125-130 on news that the company had received an offer from a private investment firm to invest $152 million in exchange for a 70 percent stake in the struggling computer wholesaler. The new funds would be used to eliminate most of the company's debt.
Under a previous proposal, bondholders would exchange their $125 million in senior notes for a large equity stake in Merisel.
"The (new deal) is a better for current stockholders and worse for bondholders," said on distressed bond trader.

The trader speculated that the new deal was likely to be approved. But he said current bondholders would probably extract concession from the company, perhaps in the form of a smaller equity stake, in exchange for giving the company flexiblity in making upcoming bond payments.

In the broader markets, traders said prices on high-grade and junk bonds remained generally unchanged. One trader said the bank sector was trading slightly tighter on recent positive news on bank earnings.
Elsewhere, the Dow Jones Industrial Average reached another all-time high, climbing 52.73 points to 7975.

Treasuries closed modestly higher after the release of a Redbook weekly survey that suggested consumer demand in early July was cooling. In the morning, the market weakened as a result of a somewhat stronger-than-expected June retail sales report.
The price of the benchmark 30-year Treasury closed 4/32 higher than Monday's closing levels. Its closing price was 101-1/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
